title: City Comparison Tool: Two Cities, Side by Side
description: Compare two cities side by side with the City Comparison Tool — population, density, area and distance on one honest table. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, New York City holds 8,804,190 people (2020 Census) against Los Angeles' 3,898,747 — 2.26 times as many people on about two-thirds of LA's land.
quick_answer: The City Comparison Tool puts two cities side by side — population, land area, density and the distance between them — using consistent definitions for both. Name the pair and read the table — same census, same boundaries, same year, so nothing compares a city to a metro by accident.

faq: City proper by default, labelled on the table — metros answer a different question (labour markets) and mixing the two in one comparison is how misleading rankings are born.
Where do the populations come from?
The national census of each city (2020 for the US examples on this page), with the year travelling with the number. Cross-country pairs compare each side's own census, years noted.
Can I compare cities in different countries?
Yes — with the caution that census years and city-boundary philosophies differ (a French commune is not a US municipality). The table labels definitions so the reader can judge.
Why does density use land area?
Water is not lived on. Density over total area (harbours included) flatters coastal cities; land-only is the honest denominator, used consistently here.
Any two places in the gazetteer compare — the measures shrink gracefully to towns, where one census's vintage matters even more.
Run pairwise tables — three-way tables invite cherry-picked rows, and the discipline of this tool is its defence against them.
Census history is fascinating and available in census archives; this tool's table is the current-vintage comparison, kept single-dated on purpose.
Costs have their own comparator on this site; climate belongs to weather records. This table is size, density and distance — the skeleton the other comparisons hang on.
